# Deploy the Terraform MCP server

This topic provides an overview of how to deploy the Terraform Model Context
Protocol (MCP) server. The Terraform MCP server enables AI models to generate
Terraform configuration using up-to-date information from the Terraform
Registry. You can also connect the server to HCP Terraform or your Terraform
Enterprise deployment. This lets you generate Terraform configuration using
artifacts from your organizations. 

 > **Hands-on**: Try the [Integrate your private module registry with the
 > Terraform MCP server
 > tutorial](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/cloud/mcp).
 > Learn how to use the Terraform MCP server to explore your HCP Terraform
 > private registry and generate Terraform configuration.

## Deployment options 

You can run the Terraform MCP server on your local machine, host it in a remote
environment that you manage, or connect to the Remote Terraform MCP server that
HashiCorp hosts.

- Local deployments are best for helping you get started or for one-off projects. Refer to [Deploy Terraform MCP server locally](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/local) for instructions.
- Self-hosted deployments are best for centrally managing the server, which helps you implement good governance policies across your organizations. Self-hosted deployments also support Terraform Enterprise. Refer to [Deploy a self-hosted Terraform MCP server](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/self-hosted) for instructions.
- The Remote Terraform MCP server is best for connecting to HCP Terraform without installing or operating a server. The Remote Terraform MCP server is in beta. Refer to [Connect to the Remote Terraform MCP server](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/remote-mcp) for instructions.

The following table compares the deployment options:

| | Local | Self-hosted | Remote MCP |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who runs the server | You, on your machine | You, in an environment you manage | HashiCorp |
| Transport | `stdio` or `streamable-http` | `streamable-http` | `streamable-http` |
| Installation | Docker, binary, or source | Docker, binary, or source | None |
| HCP Terraform | Supported | Supported | Supported, requires an API token |
| Terraform Enterprise | Supported | Supported | Not supported |
| Server configuration | You control it | You control it | HashiCorp controls it |

## Secure configuration

Implement the following recommendations to securely deploy a local or
self-hosted MCP server. HashiCorp manages the configuration of the Remote
Terraform MCP server. Refer to [Remote Terraform MCP server
security](/terraform/mcp-server/security#remote-terraform-mcp-server-security)
for more information.

- **Hosting**: We recommend running the MCP server locally at `127.0.0.1` through the STDIO or HTTP Streamable transport protocol to limit publicly exposing your Terraform environment. The default transport is set to STDIO. If you host the service remotely, we recommend implementing additional security controls at the application and network layers. For example, you can add an API gateway with authentication, TLS encryption, and IP whitelisting between the client and server.
- **CORS**: By default, Terraform MCP server runs in `strict` CORS (cross-origin request) mode and the allowed origins are empty. As a result, all cross-origin requests are blocked unless the server is explicitly configured to allow them. Exercise caution when changing the allowed origins list.
- **Terraform authentication**: The `TFE_SKIP_TLS_VERIFY` option is set to `false` by default so that the MCP server verifies that the HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise TLS certificate is valid. If you temporarily set this option to `true` for testing or other use cases, we strongly recommend resetting to `false` to ensure that encryption is enabled. We also recommend limiting the permissions of the `TFE_TOKEN` used to authenticate as described in the Terraform documentation. Refer to [API tokens](/terraform/cloud-docs/users-teams-organizations/api-tokens) for more information.
- **Rate limiting**: We recommend setting up global and per-session rate limits to prevent the server or dependent resources from becoming overloaded through excessive requests. 
- **TLS**: When making your MCP server accessible remotely, we recommend adding TLS certificates to the host infrastructure to protect in-transit communication. To serve HTTPS from the server itself, set the `MCP_TLS_CERT_FILE` and `MCP_TLS_KEY_FILE` environment variables. Refer to [Configure TLS](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/self-hosted#configure-tls) for more information.
- **Organization allowlist**: When you host the server remotely, we recommend restricting access to the organizations that you expect to use the server. Refer to [Restrict access by organization](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/self-hosted#restrict-access-by-organization) for more information.

## Authentication

Terraform MCP server v0.3.0 or newer is required to authenticate with the Terraform registry. You must also obtain an authentication token from HCP Terraform or your Terraform Enterprise deployment so that the MCP server can access your private registry. Refer to [API tokens](/terraform/cloud-docs/users-teams-organizations/api-tokens) for instructions.

We recommend authenticating the server with HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise so that you can interact with your organization and private registry. Refer to [Connect to HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/local#connect-to-hcp-terraform-or-terraform-enterprise) for more information.

The Remote Terraform MCP server requires an HCP Terraform API token for every request. We recommend using a user API token. Refer to [Create an API token](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/remote-mcp#create-an-api-token) for more information.
